title: Terrible Times and God-Breathed Scripture
summary: Paul warns that the last days will bring terrible times, marked by people who love themselves, money, and pleasure more than God and who keep a form of godliness while denying its power. Such people, like Pharaoh's magicians Jannes and Jambres, oppose the truth but will not get far. Paul reminds Timothy of his own teaching and persecutions, warns that all who want to live godly lives in Christ will be persecuted, and urges him to continue in the Holy Scriptures, which are God-breathed and useful to equip the servant of God for every good work.
story: The first two chapters of the letter called Timothy to courage and to faithful teaching. Chapter 3 widens the view to the times in which he must minister. The false teachers in Ephesus are not an isolated problem but a sign of the last days, which the New Testament understands as the whole period between Christ's first coming and his return. Against that dark background Paul sets two resources: the example of his own life, which Timothy has watched closely, and the Scriptures, which Timothy has known since he was a child. This chapter contains the New Testament's most direct statement about the nature of Scripture, and it comes not as abstract theory but as equipment for a young leader in a hard place.
historical:
The persecutions Paul lists in verse 11 took place in cities of southern Galatia in Asia Minor on his first missionary trip (Acts 13:14-14:20). In Pisidian Antioch, opponents stirred up leading citizens and drove Paul and Barnabas out; in Iconium there was a plot to stone them; in Lystra, Timothy's hometown, Paul was stoned and left for dead. Timothy may have witnessed some of this as a young man, and it was in that region that he joined Paul soon afterward (Acts 16:1-3). Paul's appeal to it is personal: Timothy knows exactly what following Christ has cost.

The Holy Scriptures Timothy knew from infancy (verse 15) were the Jewish Scriptures, what Christians call the Old Testament, which he would have learned from his mother and grandmother (1:5). At the time the letter was written, the New Testament had not yet been gathered, though Paul's letters were already circulating, and 2 Peter 3:15-16 groups them with the other Scriptures. The church has always understood Paul's statement about all Scripture to apply to the whole canon as it came to be recognized.
cultural:
Jannes and Jambres (verse 8) are not named in the Old Testament. Exodus 7:11 speaks only of the magicians of Egypt who imitated Moses' signs, but Jewish tradition gave them names, and forms of these names appear in later Jewish writings, including the Aramaic paraphrases of Scripture called the Targums, and in the Damascus Document known from the Dead Sea Scrolls. Paul draws on this well-known tradition to make his point: the opponents imitate true power but are exposed in the end, as Pharaoh's magicians were.

The list of vices in verses 2-5 resembles lists found in Greek moral writing and elsewhere in Paul (Romans 1:29-31). What is striking is the frame: it begins with lovers of self and lovers of money and ends with lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God. Misdirected love is the root of the whole list. The teachers who worm their way into households (verse 6) reflect the fact that the church met in homes, and that teachers could gain influence by visiting households, especially while men were away at work. Paul's description of the women they influenced is not a statement about women in general but about particular people burdened by sin and drawn to endless learning that never arrived at the truth.
literary: The chapter has two parts joined by a sharp contrast. Verses 1-9 describe the people of the last days in a long list of eighteen descriptions, many built from the same few Greek elements (words beginning with phil-, love of, and with a-, meaning without), followed by a command to avoid them, a portrait of their methods, and a comparison with Jannes and Jambres. Verse 10 turns with “You, however” to Timothy, and verses 10-17 set out what he has that they lack: an example to follow (10-13) and the Scriptures to continue in (14-17). The final two verses build to a climax: Scripture is God-breathed, useful for four purposes (instruction, conviction, correction, training), with the result that the man of God is complete and fully equipped. The repetition of equipment language (complete, fully equipped) stresses sufficiency.

outline.t: Terrible times: lovers of self, money, and pleasure
Deceivers in households, like Jannes and Jambres
Paul's example and the certainty of persecution

doctrines.note: “All Scripture is God-breathed” (verse 16). Scripture has its origin in God; it is his word, given through human writers, and therefore it carries his authority. It is able to make a person “wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (verse 15) and to equip God's servant “for every good work” (verse 17). This is the church's confession about the Bible, grounded in the Bible's own witness.

“All who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (verse 12). Persecution is not a sign that something has gone wrong but a normal mark of faithfulness in a world that opposes the truth.

The vices of verses 2-4 are framed by disordered loves: of self, of money, of pleasure, rather than of God. Idolatry here is not bowing to statues but loving created things in God's place, while keeping a form of godliness.

words.note: Theopneustos, God-breathed. This is the word's first known appearance in Greek, and it may have been coined for this purpose. It does not mean that God breathed into existing writings to make them inspiring, but that Scripture is breathed out by God, the product of his creative breath (compare Psalm 33:6, where the heavens are made by the breath of his mouth). The word states Scripture's origin, and its origin grounds its authority.

Graphē, a writing, and in the New Testament the regular word for Scripture. “All Scripture” in verse 16 could also be translated every Scripture, meaning each part of it. A few translations have rendered the verse as saying that every God-breathed Scripture is also useful, but most translators and interpreters read it as a statement that all Scripture is God-breathed.

Morphōsis, form or outward shape. In verse 5 the people of the last days have “a form of godliness but denying its power”: the outward appearance of religion without the reality. Paul uses the same word positively in Romans 2:20 for the embodiment of knowledge in the law.

Exartizō, to equip fully or furnish completely. It was used of fitting out a ship for a voyage or supplying a workman with tools. Scripture makes the man of God “fully equipped for every good work” (verse 17), which is the basis for the church's confession of Scripture's sufficiency.

christ: Paul says the Scriptures are able to make Timothy “wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (verse 15). This is how the New Testament reads the Old: not as a collection of rules or a book of timeless wisdom detached from Jesus, but as a witness that leads to faith in him. Jesus himself said the Scriptures testify about him (John 5:39) and opened them to his disciples after his resurrection (Luke 24:27). The persecution Paul describes follows the pattern of Christ's own life: all who desire to live godly lives “in Christ Jesus” will suffer as he did (verse 12). And the Lord who rescued Paul from all his persecutions (verse 11) is the risen Christ, present with his servants.

hard.q: If Scripture is God-breathed, were the human writers simply taking dictation?
hard.a:
The church has confessed from the beginning that Scripture is God's word, as this verse plainly states. It has also recognized that Scripture is fully human: its books show the vocabulary, style, personality, and circumstances of their writers, from Paul's personal requests for his cloak and books to Luke's careful research (Luke 1:1-4). Very few Christian thinkers have held that the writers were passive secretaries. The usual understanding, which 2 Peter 1:21 supports when it says the prophets spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit, is that God worked through the writers' own minds and personalities so that what they wrote was what he intended.

Christians who share this confession have described its implications in different terms. Many hold that Scripture is inerrant, without error in all that it affirms. Others prefer to say it is infallible, wholly trustworthy for its purpose of making people wise for salvation and equipping them for good works, and they locate apparent difficulties in human transmission or in misreading the text's genre. These are important differences, but they are differences within a shared confession that Scripture comes from God and carries his authority.

questions: The vice list is framed by misplaced loves: of self, money, and pleasure. Which of these competes most with love for God in your own life?
Paul points Timothy to his example and to Scripture. Who has been an example of faithfulness for you, and how did you learn from watching them?
Paul says Scripture is useful for instruction, conviction, correction, and training. Which of those four do you most often skip, and why?
